Pros:
- Art style is interesting and engaging
- Story is well crafted and immersive
- Exposition isn't forced on you, but it is there if you wish to learn more about the world or certain characters
- Creators clearly spent a lot of time and effort on the setting 
- The game tackles some pretty engaging ethical dilemas that are applicable to the world we live in

Cons:
- Click and drag simulator 2016
- Uninspired gameplay mechanics 
- Constant handholding (I kept thinking I was in a long tutorial but that's just how the game is)
- Very binary choices (he did it vs she did it/ she did the right thing vs she is bad)
- No real detective work the game just tells you everything
- The game treats you like an idiot by having a sidekick tell you what each piece of info means


Other things that bothered me:

-      Chat/phone calls move too fast to keep up with uploading the 'chunks' that appear and you're forced to either ignore the dialogue progression and try to click on a certain chuck as the screen constantly shifts or wait until the exchange is  done to upload anything (or maybe I was just too slow).

-      Music shifts in tone dramtically whenever 'shocking info' is revealed which makes the game feel very linear (which it is) instead of just letting you stumble upon the info yourself and make your own conclusions as to what is important. The music changes give the feeling of "This was a scripted event that I experienced at a designated time."

-      Your partner/boss just tells you things so you don't really have to do any investigation yourself which is kind the whole point of the game. 

-      You are fed information in a pretty constant chronological stream instead being given all the info at once and having to sort through it with your brain. The game treats you like a baby and doesn't give you your next treat until you click and drag the things on the page it just gave you. 

-      The game established this rhythm really early of scrolling through a page, clicking on stuff, listening to your buddy pal guy tell you stuff, being given a new page, then repeating.

-      The fact that the chats/calls don't start until you actively bring them up is quite harmful to immersion (why would the people wait to start talking on the phone for 5 seconds until I'm monitoring them? Just have them act like normal humans and not wait for the player).

-      The gameplay would be a lot better if the events driving the characters weren't so close to the present. If we as players were given this new technology to help solve a crime in the past (several months at least) it would eliminate the need to have these awfully convenient text conversations and phone calls every 5 seconds that always have important info. What I'm saying is put the event in the past so that the player can be given a bunch of call transcripts and chat logs to sift through instead of being handed the info.

-      The very nature of how the game highlights all of the important info for you makes you question what your job really is and why anyone would need you to do it. If they already have a system that determines what is important and human operators who interpret the data (your boss/partner guy), why the hell do they need you???

-      The info highlighting eventually has you just scrolling through pages until something lights up or you get an update instead of actually reading the page and deciding what is important and what is irrelevant.




This is not a bad game by any means. It's just always frustrating when I see one of these "choices matter" games where there's clearly a certain path you're encouraged to take and you really aren't free to do things your own way.

While I had pretty high expectations for this game after coming off a Hacknet binge, I just feel as though the game is trying to pretend to be something it's not. Just market the game for what it is, a linear narrative experience.

I'm very aware that since I did not finish the game my perspective is limited to what I played, but what I played I did not enjoy, so I cannot reccomend this game.

TL;DR: This game is a very and hand-holdy linear story based experience while it is advertised to be a sort of detective

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
If there were a "maybe" option for recommending this game I would have given it that, but with only a "yes" or "no" choice unfortunately I have to just come down on the side of the latter.

This game is essentially a "choose your own adventure" detective novel wherein your decisions are all made by choosing which information to share with - or conceal from - the authorities. The concept is an interesting one and the game does throw up some nice surprises in both the gameplay and the plot, and there are occasional moments of humour.

However, the limitations in using conflicting information are rather annoying. For example sometimes the game will let you choose only one of two (or more) different pieces of information even when both are true and could be vital to successfully completing your objectives. (I get that this is a key game mechanic, but I think it could be explained or handled better to make the game feel less forced.) In particular there is one key decision which just comes down to a 50/50 guess with no supporting information to help the player make the correct choice. (I am talking about the part where the player must determine the third location - If I missed any clues as to which is the correct answer, somebody please tell me!)

Another major concern is the quality of the writing; whilst for the most part the writing is capable and there are some memorable moments, the writing is never compelling - I gave up reading about halfway through my first playthrough, instead just scanning text for the (conveniently highlighted) choices. Whilst I can forgive bad writing in some games, for a game that is all about the writing the standard really needs to be higher. Some of the text simply drags on too long, especially any form of dialogue (phone calls, chat text, etc.) - this is doubly annoying for dialogue as there is no way to skip it. (Usually you can just let it run in the background whilst you read other in-game documents, but be careful with this as some actions are time-critical.)

Replay value may depend how willing you are to work through the text again. Whilst it is nice to see the different outcomes your actions can have, it feels like 90% or more of the game remains identical so it becomes a slog to see the few changes or pick up achievements. Some of the achievements are so ambiguously described that the only way to complete them seems to be relying on lots of replays and blind luck, or of course walkthroughs.

It is a shame to see such a nice idea and plot wasted without sufficient polish, but if the devs learn from this I do look forward to seeing what else they can produce.

review_text_raw:
TL:DR, I myself enjoyed this game, great if you are into detective type work. Not a super exciting but overall 7/10

For the record, I got this while on sale for 5 dollars during steam sales. I see normally priced at 10 and that would be a maybe for buying it. 

So by the title you can guess that this has to do with big brother type surveillance, but in this you are acting as the investigator using the big brother program aka Orwell as a tool to piece together the story as it is happening about a alleged terrorist group. I can definitely see where someone could play this and find it dull and boring, but for me personally I found it intriguing and fun being able to access files and eavesdrop on conversation and collect intel from all sources. As well as building up character profiles and finding the relationships. One of few complaints I have is the moral dillema is kinda thrown in your face in the last moments of the game, which didn't ruin the game for me because it does then offer you a choice, but just felt very uninspired in a sense. The story leading to it was all around pretty good. While character development was great at times and very stereotypical in other times, the act of putting together character history and connections is actual quite fun. Especially in a sense where going through my first play through seemed to not matter and as though it seemed straight forward, looking at the achievements afterward and noticing I am missing half of them. And looking at the details of the achievements I can see where my actions can affect the story through the game. Similar to the character development, the story plot points were mostly good, but lack luster in other times. 

Gameplay itself feels immersive to me, but dont go into this expecting a whole bunch of mechanics or crazy things you can do. You are essentially sitting on a computer screen doing research and hacking into things. 

I will say, I went into this expecting there to be different cases as well, not to say I was dissapointed, I just thought there would be more to the game itself.

For 5 bucks and the first run through taking only 3 hours to complete I would recommend it, and I might go through again to see if I can knock out the other achievements and to really see what affect I have on the game.

review_text_raw:
ORWELL is a hybrid game somewhere between visual novel and point and click adventure. In the game, you are an investigator hired by the nation in testing out a new law which allows the government to spy on its citizens in order to find criminals. While this doesn’t sound too far off from where we are today, we can assume ordinary citizens aren’t having their wires tapped and all their online activity personally searched into. But that blurred line between what in this game is fiction and what is potential reality is where the game really shines, and pushes me to giving this game a general recommendation.
ORWELL starts off with investigating into a bomb that went off on a popular plaza and investigating a person of interest who was at the plaza. This is the only cutscene in the game and I really need to say that it shows how ugly the art style is. ORWELL has this odd polygonal art style that just doesn’t look right, and the game does nothing to utilize the style as well. Take a game like Wind Waker and the cell shading is important to the overall feel of the game, and the entire game would be very different if they had gone in a more realistic style. The reason I recommend it is because of that blurred line I mentioned at the beginning. You can’t help but think if someone were to investigate me, they would find my screennames, my posts all over the internet, my video replays from streaming, and could trace words I said years ago to implicate me in something I was not a part of.

But playing through everything and seeing how everything plays out is thrilling in a way that no other game has ever provided for me. There is an ORWELL season 2 planned, and if they could just step away from the source material and feel more liberty to explore the world they’ve gone ahead and made, a lot of the issues I have with season 1 would be rectified. Overall, a 7/10. If you like dystopian media and the thought be being a voyeur into the lives of the ordinary citizens, give it a shot.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] Game Summary: [/h1] 
This game doesn't fit into most normal game conventions and acts more like a cautionary tale.  By allowing the gamer to take the seat of a possible government agent in a program giving you so much power and access over people's lives, it lets you determine what you take away from it.  Is it a necessary evil for the government to have this much depth and access to what people are posting online, downloaded on their various devices, and talking about in their phone calls?  Or is that question alone already pushing too far, as people have an inherent right to privacy?  Wisely the game developer merely posits this to its audience, instead of preaching what is or isn't appropriate behavior in the 21st Century and beyond.  


[h1] Pros: [/h1] 
•	The first playthrough where I was intruding so far into people's lives made me feel uncomfortable.  Not scared or tense, just somewhat uncomfortable.  I think it's because invading people's privacy to this extent, knowing how easily the same thing could happen to you, is rather unsettling.  Medical records and mental health histories, various profiles and online communities you participate in (theoretically behind an alias), personal conversations and chats, all available for someone to read through.  For someone to comb through for any signs of instability, derangement, or evidence that this person isn't a law-abiding citizen, but a dirty crook.  This is dangerously close to criminalizing people for wrong-think.  
•	This game shines in its story and writing, because the characters feel real.  Their various profiles and conversations, how they become both paranoid and angry, but still only guessing at how bad things already are regarding the government's intrusion into their lives.  It gives the game a greater sense of reality and immersion, which is key.  They may not be rocket scientists, but they do take steps to avoid being screwed over, though if you're being a good big brother, it's already too late for them.  
•	I love that what I choose to upload can have a pretty big impact on how what the characters are saying and doing is interpreted.  It can either be seen as the acts of an innocent person, or the pattern of someone who's a low-down crook.  It raises the question of how any of us would look from the outside to someone who'd see all of our online activity.
•	The music acts as ambient background.  It's very low-key, and could theoretically be the sort of soft tune a government office would play to keep employees from getting too antsy.  This is for the most part, but when the climax of each day/act builds, then it picks up and gets you on edge.


[h1] Cons: [/h1] 
• 	Though it would take more time in both development and gameplay, it'd be nice if there were more people for you to look into who turned out to be red herrings.  It's not necessarily enjoyable being led astray, but it'd help sharpen the point of the game.  If you were being paranoid and looking at people through the lens of criminalizing everyone, you'd waste time and resources chasing false leads.  If you put on kids gloves and rationalized every viable threat as a misunderstanding, you'd let dangerous people slip on through.  What people say and mean aren't always the same, and one person's harmless rant is another's death threat.  
•	*Semi-Spoiler* I think one downside of the story is that all the key players are not inherently innocent.  They all have something significant to cover up, a reasonable way of implicating them for a crime and leading to their detention.  If they were merely guilty by association, and small phrases and statements were being pulled together to paint them as guilty, I think that would have had a stronger impact.  Otherwise, with how it is here, locking everybody up is justified.  You aren't throwing someone in jail who's wholly innocent.
•	Ironically, with how the last day plays out, you get so much material to look at, but are strictly limited on how much you can upload.  I get the idea of building tension this way, but I think it goes against what the game was going for.  The dilemma of the game wasn't in having to make a decision with so little information, but at digging for far too much, and falsely implicating innocent people on what you could piece together.  
•	Where the game suffers is through further playthroughs, as you see what happens if you try things a bit differently.  Since you're familiar with the characters, storyline, and reading their messages, it'd be nice if those could be sped up, instead of having to wait.  The chats are fairly crisp-paced considering they're supposed to be happening real-time, but it bogs down when you've seen it before.
•	Early in the game, video footage was used, and I thought that was going to come up again later.  I was quite disappointed that it only had a place in the game once, and I do feel misled that everything you analyze in the game is just text, whether a call, chat, or profile.
•	It'd be nice if some of the items which are definitively pointless and not useful anymore would be cleared away.  For instance, all the random news clips and headlines, since most of them had no pertinence to the exploration for more information.  
•	Sometimes I had a really hard time dragging points of interest into profiles or disabling them.  The controls were a bit floaty and annoying to work with.


[h1] Conclusion: [/h1] 
Whether we like it or not, whatever we post online is going to exist indefinitely.  Since so much information is out there, it does raise the issue of who would be keeping track of these matters, who might be lurking without our knowledge to try and keep tabs over us.  Whether it's the government or not, people can do some pretty sketchy things with computers, and this knowledge and power is a great temptation, tool, and force.  This game acts as a simulation for what can be done with that kind of power.  A bumbling buffoon who doesn't take it seriously, could allow guilty parties to slip out of facing justice.  An overly authoritarian and distrustful person could throw people behind bars for any minor infraction.  True, laws may have been broken, but should we throw away privacy and autonomy to catch such small fries?  We'd be foolish to hand over such power carelessly, as it could be so easily abused, but total restriction could also prevent heinous monsters from being caught and prosecuted.  These are hefty matters worthy of being discussed in the public sphere, and this game highlights both sides of that discussion.  If you're looking for a game in a conventional sense, you'd be disappointed, but if you're open to an experience with an important message at its core, Orwell has a lot to offer.  

Be careful if you write a reply or comment on this review.  You don't know who could be reading it.  It's alright if you don't necessarily agree with everything the government does, but don't be overly critical and certainly don't call for a revolution or anything CRAZY like that.  We'd HATE for there to be a group trying to overthrow the government, right?  Oh crap, I hear them at my door.  They're on to me!  Fight while you still can, don't be compliant, resist, fight on, fi-!  *Device has been disconnected*

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Excellent game.

To those who know the references and like the source material this game is based off of, this is perhaps the best Big Brother/Orwellian Surveillance system simulator I've seen so far, and is well worth the price its asking for. 

Fans of Papers, Please will probably enjoy this game just as much. Except instead of being the Border Crossing Guard, think of yourself as the Investigator for their Surveillance Corps.

Its a short game, sure, you can beat it once probably within 4 hours, but it does have some replayability (plus the fact that there is no hard save points, the game constantly saves after everything you do with no way of going back outside of making a new profile, so it forces you to choose wisely). To me, the shortness is forgiveable for how much this game costs (which isn't much).

The writing is amazing for it being a game with only written dialogue, the characters feel real and individual and you're the spider trying to weave out the web of how they fit into the plot that's going on. It also does a great job of getting you into the role of being an Investigator of a secret service public spying agency, you feel as if you're in the game just as much as any of them at times.

The art style is consistent and works for the game that this is, but IMO they could have had clear photos and models and you would have had the same game, this style merely gives it a more individual feel rather than it being like any other game like this.

The gameplay is simple, but great if you're into investigative puzzle-solving.

The music is very good for eliciting responses and making you feel certain emotions at particular times, as its supposed to, though IMO it moves a little too fast at times in transitions. You're often left with an abrupt music cue and wondering "What the hell, what did I just find?" before you can properly read what found. But otherwise its good.

Only encountered one bug at the very end of the game where it froze and looped the last second or two of the music track I was listening to, and I had to exit out with alt-tab, but I had beaten the playthrough by that point so it wasn't a huge deal.

All and all, a great game for the price its asking for, and if you're a fan of the type of genre this is.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
The premise is interesting, the UI is fantastic, but...

The writing doesn't work. Not to me, at least.

So the idea is, you're an anonymous member of the public working with a new program that's half google, half snooping software. You're assigned a case - the first one is about a bomb placed in a plaza, and thanks to surveillance cameras you're assigned to look up everything about a suspect. So far so good, right? There's the relevant question of whether it's right to spy on someone in the name of public safety, there's a mystery to solve...

But it falls apart. Your supervisor is all "she has a police record, let's snoop on her" and okay, good enough reason to investigate...her faux-facebook page, her faux-portfolio, news websites, etcetera. Except that none of these websites feel like they were ever used by real people, her facebook timeline feels bizarre, like she's a fascimile of a human being, and when you get to eavesdrop on her text messages with her boyfriend, again it feels false?

Everything is off, and not in a good way. And your supervisor is so ready to pin the entire case on her because she's joined an activist group that organizes protests against the surveillance state.

It's too on the nose, with writing that doesn't sell to me that I'm snooping on real people, with a wonky "this is taking place in real time" - but it's not, really, you only get to eavesdrop on people's text conversations when you unlock them, not when they happen - and it all just feels clumsy.

In a game that's only got its writing going for it, having a fantastically slick UI isn't going to keep me playing it. Which is a bummer! The questions this game is asking are relevant, and it's so slick and pretty to look at I want to dig into it! ... But sadly it's just not compelling.

Bummer.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This game will have you be FBI in a world where the NSA collects and store [i]everything[/i] but doesn't share it with you.

First off I rarely do reviews here on Steam but this game deserves it. Not because it's inherently bad game design, I don't think it is so much. Not because I just personally didn't like it or anything like that. I actually enjoyed the design choices both in terms of gameplay and aesthetics, it just works as is, nothing great but nothing terrible either. I have to review this and end up not recommending it because it's not even close to anything worth being called "Orwell". It's just not Orwellian enough, not thought-provocative enough. If you want to experience something more Orwellian just sign up on Facebook right now if you don't already have an account. It's even [i]"free"[/i]!

This game is overall a good piece of interactive narrative that can get you thinking about the implications of indiscriminately sharing every last little tidbit surrounding your life, and how that which you choose to share, along with other information available out there about yourself, can and will be used to create an image of you that might not necessarily be the whole picture. It's also good social commentary on the whole deal surrounding what makes an actual terrorist in today's world; This is immediately apparent as protesters early in the game protesting against mass surveillance because, well, mass surveillance, are portrayed as "anti-governmental terrorists" without much more context to legitimize that label.

You're the In-Between Brother, looking down on Little Brother, bossing him around; But in the end both you and Little Brother are in a complete chokehold by Big Brother - no match, not even close.

What I'm trying to say is that this game does a good job of portraying how [b]directed surveillance[/b], what could be considered actual legit surveillance techniques, can be used to make decisions on who to pin crimes on after the fact. The game specifically portrays collection of information from social media as self-publicized, along with information gathered in general around the whole internet about a person, as this information is available when [b]specifically being looked for[/b]. That last part make a world of a difference. If a social media post has been removed by a user in this Orwellian future, well guess what, Big Brother can't see that post either. Orwellian, isn't it? Provocative, isn't it? 

The game does make some thought-provocative points around this theme of directed surveillance and social media content and in general hits the spot on that. In this day and age however it just isn't Orwellian enough, as what we have in our society today in terms of actual massive surveillance capabilities far surpasses anything remotely portrayed in this game.

So in conclusion, if you happen to feel that Big Brother-urge grow in you and all you want is to see how you would conduct yourself on the other side of the fence looking down on the sheeple, well look elsewhere. This won't be your fix. If you on the other hand feel like doing some detective work in a social media/online context and occasionally pin crimes on innocents for those authoritarian kicks, this might be your fix after all!

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This one's a "buy it only on sale" for me. I would pick a neutral option were it available.

It's important to understand that Orwell is not a puzzle game inasmuch as a visual novel, and from what I understand of Steam's userbase (or at least its most vocal negative reviews), this will come as a disappointment to some people. There is very little analysis involved; you are told what and whom to investigate and any conclusions about what you discover are more or less made for you. Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You also fairly short for a $10 title, with very little replayability. Halfway through the game I still thought I was in the tutorial until I glanced at the list of achievements which indicated otherwise.

In Orwell, you are tasked with finding the culprit of a recent bombing using a top secret surveillance system also called ORWELL. Specifically, you must build profiles of potential suspects based on their social media profiles, online accounts, and personal devices. This is done by selecting relevant excerpts, called datachunks, and "uploading" them to the ORWELL server. Meanwhile, your "advisor," a man called Symes, will review what you send and make important decisions based on this info. What information you choose to upload and when you upload it will affect the lives of the people you investigate and the dangerous events unfolding in "real time."

Unfortunately, your advisor is an idiot. I mean, he seems nice enough, but he's incredibly trigger-happy, and views the act of merely uploading information to compile a detailed suspect profile as an indictment in itself. "Woah, she changed her hair color? Good info, I've just sent out the warrant for her arrest."

Because of this and other aspects of gameplay where the importance of particular actions is not especially well telegraphed, most of my game-changing decisions were followed by an "oh crap, I did not just mean to do that. I hope I can fix it later!"

When control over a sandbox environment and its inhabitants is so apparently arbitrary, your first playthrough is no longer a personal journey and a reflection of your choices. Instead it is a hilarious spectacle of disastrous butterfly effects outpacing your sad and frantic attempts at damage control. This is great in a series like Hitman, though not so much in a game trying to make a point about the deadly shortsightedness of relying on a digital panopticon.

Orwell's conceit is ultimately that even a government allowed to so thoroughly investigate its private citizens may still fail to meet the outcomes that were supposed to justify the dissolution of privacy. The truth can still elude even the most advanced surveillance systems, as it does here, and so any drastic actions carried out in the name of safety may do more harm than good.

The problem is that it tries to demonstrate this through a system made deliberately inept in the service of its plot and political message. EDIT: So I'm an idiot and apparently you can arrest the true mastermind in Episode 5 provided you have enough luck and/or second playthrough foresight. However, it's not especially intuitive (the 20 datachunk limit doesn't help!), and requires some deviation from the stated goal in a game which has been so far entirely based on completing the stated goal in some form or another and which otherwise restricts your ability to freely investigate, in that:

ORWELL will only allow access to new resources once you have added a related datachunk, and even then this selection is limited by what the clumsy "AI" (read: the story) deems relevant. The AI also determines which pieces of information are selectable for use as datachunks. The result is like a crime-solving version of Chopped, wherein you must come up with your best answer given a random handful of documents. You are only able to pursue a line of thinking that the AI believes is relevant, and the AI has been written to provide the wrong answer.

You can't get much out of the stuff you're forced to work with, either, as advisors will only let you investigate people they deem worthy at the time (rest assured you will still get the blame every time something bad happens!), and with each datachunk you index in the hopes of unlocking new documents or comments, you run the risk of your advisor making an unpredictably dangerous and irreversible decision.

As a result, Orwell depicts not so much the shortcomings of overly-invasive surveillance tech as it does the flaws in this particular system which has been deliberately badly designed.

Usually writers in the "techno-voyeurism genre" can look forward to populating a lot of fake apps and web pages with filler data which serves no plot purpose except to flesh out the in-game universe and hide easter eggs. So I understand the choice for the developers to omit that open browsing capability from a practical point of view -- but it does come at a cost to Orwell's credibility.

On the positive side, Orwell has a cute low-poly aesthetic and its UI is both visually appealing and well organized, especially given what a tremendous challenge it must have been to elegantly display so much information. The soundtrack works well and effectively manages to convey dramatic tone shifts (usually from "lalala browsing someone's timeline" to "oh NO A BOMB IS ABOUT TO GO OFF IN THIRTY SECONDS!!"). I also like that there are achievements of equal calibre for most major story outcomes, "good" or otherwise.

By all means get Orwell if you enjoy techno-voyeurism (does this genre have an actual name?); you might find it to be a fun time-waster. I might pick up season 2... on sale... eventually. I just don't think it would appeal to general audiences at its current price point, or that it's particularly effective in delivering its themes.

[h1]Overall Rating[/h1] 
[b]★★☆☆☆[/b]

[u]What I liked[/u]
[list]
  [*] The Story
  [*] The Character Building
[/list]

[u]What I didn't like[/u]
[list]
  [*] The UI/UX
  [*] The Gameplay 
  [*] The replayability 
[/list]

[h1]Review[/h1]

 In Orwell you are an investigator, you need to investigate what might be a terrorist attack, and find the culprit(s). You can check people's background, access their emails, listen to their phone conversations or access their electronic devices. You can choose not to inform what you find to orwell or frame someone so he or she goes to jail.
 There are a couple of different endings, for both the story and the characters (including you, of course). Not all are happy.

[u]Why I liked[/u]
[list]
  [*] The Story: Is really rich, and depending on your choices, full of plot twists.
  [*] The Character Building: All the characters are really well written, how they interact between each other, and their personalities. I in part, what makes the story rich
[/list]

[u]Why didn't like[/u]
[list]
  [*] The UI/UX: You have an annoying companion, that cannot be disabled, that makes annoying comments about the data you upload. The uploading process could be faster also, I understand it tries to simulate a real computer connected to internet, but still it could be faster.
  [*] The Gameplay: Even though your choices matter, there are not a lot of choices you can make. All the data-chunks get highlighted, and the only options you have, are either uploading the information, or not. There's really no challenge, and probably by the third episode, you'll just be looking for highlighted text.
  [*] The replayability: I got all the Achievements in about 28 hours, and completed the game 4 times in that time, exploring all the endings.
[/list]

[h1]Bottom Line[h1]
 I thought I was going to find something different, something I could replay once and again. I really think the game has a lot of potential, but I can't recommend it.

review_text_raw:
I think I got this for free some months ago and now got to play it. It ran rather fine on an Ubuntu 18.04 lapttop with Nouveau drivers, game has native Linux support. 
You play as a worker for a surveillance program, sorting through the web and accessing peoples devices, looking for clues about terrorists. I cant really compare the game to anything, maybe it is similar to a graphical novel to some extent, as you have limited choices, but you do have to use your head, even if the game pretty much always at least tells you where to look for clues.  
It was almost an initimate experience to look into the character life, their private chats and calls. I feel like they could have added a bit more "useless" webpages, to make the game more authentic, but it is obvious that they tried  to give their characters depth, which is where the game shines. 
As the name of the game tells us, to some extent it is obviously a political/ethical game, even if done rather abstract (you work for "the nation", and pretty much everyone you investigate did something wrong). 
One thing I really appreciated, was that they show what can happen if systems like this make mistakes, which is something I feel like is not discussed enough as a counterargument to surveillance, besides the obvious ethical ones.  Overall the the game is an interesting experience, but not comparable to games like "Spec Ops -  The Line", where you really have to get your hands dirty, which lessens the impression of consequences of the players actions in my opinion.

review_text_raw:
[h1] How far are you willing to go to protect the populace? [/h1]

[i]Orwell[/i] is a “visual novel” style game in which you have the ability to follow cyber-breadcrumbs in order to slowly uncover suspect’s online lives. Your goal? Stop a terrorist organization (?) from bombing public spaces. Your tools? As an agent, you are privy to the entirety of your target’s posts, articles, phone calls, emails, etc. Use this information to reveal more and more relevant webpages and conversations. The catch? You’re overlooked by a supervisor and you must choose what information to upload. This supervisor can only see the bits of information you feed him, so choose wisely or risk ruining an innocent’s life. The challenge? Upload only enough information to gain new leads, but not jump to conclusions. 

Are you really helping the greater good by invading the privacy of the few? Or have you caused more harm than good, muddling in affairs you should have never been in? Are the internet spies of today, really the superheroes of tomorrow? Find out by stepping into these large, cyber shoes. Act quickly and stop a harmful event in its tracks, or wait it out and discover it was a false alarm. Big brother is watching you. You are watching the people. Lives are on the line. Decide. 

Then watch as you say, [b]“I never meant for this to happen.”[/b]

Let me start off this review by saying I’m one who really enjoys a story-based game. I particularly enjoy consequence based story games (like [i]Telltale[/i]). If that’s not your cup of tea, this game is not for you. If you’re still interested, here’s the pros and cons for the game so far.

[h1]Pros:[/h1] [b]Interesting social commentary.[/b] There’s no denying that this is the age of technology, and with that comes a whole new slew of problems that our forefathers never could have foresaw when drafting the constitution. [i]Orwell[/i] heavily and obviously alludes to the current hot topics of freedom of internet access, government access to our personal files and correspondences, and general cyber security we see crop up in the news time and time again. 

[b]Easy interface.[/b] There’s not much to learn but drag and drop. Your un-uploaded data chunks are marked so you don’t lose track of what you’ve read, need to read, and are saving for later.

[b]More unique game flow.[/b] Events don’t happen unless you upload data chucks, leaving you to explore the branches of plot in whatever order feels natural to you. It does still feel a bit restricted, though, (see “A bit linear, limited” in cons) a perhaps more of a pseudo-free-directional choice. (But isn’t the concept of freedom what this game is all about?) 

[b]Intriguing artwork.[/b] The geometric artistic style lends itself to unconsciously nod its head towards the cyber-oriented world of the game. It ties in beautifully to the theme of the game—from the logo to the interface—without being too aggressive.

[h1]Cons:[/h1] [strike][b]A better save system!![/b][/strike] Update has added a rewind system, but I have not played since [strike]I cannot stress this enough. Since this is a consequence-based game, I’d like to be able to start from the end episode one, or so, with my decisions staying the same, and only make changes to my decisions from there out, with my profiles branching out from my first play through plot line. Starting over from the beginning is too much of a grind. Even a way to speed up messaging/call text on the second (and beyond) playthrough would be better for acheivement hunters or people just curious about the other endings. Examples of games with a good save system for this style of gameplay include [i]A Wolf Among Us[/i] and [i]Papers, Please.[/i][/strike]

[b]A bit linear, limited.[/b] There were some moments I wish some bit of text was highlighted (you may only drag and upload highlighted data chunks) since I wanted to explore that avenue of inquiry, but [i]Orwell[/i] had other plans. This gave the game a restricted feeling. It does not leave the game open to a world of naturally-occurring red herrings (only game-constructed ones, not user constructed), which I think would have added much more depth to the game. Also, it’s glaringly obvious which pieces of text carry great significance. (Those will be the ones with conflicting evidence) so sometimes the challenge of deciding to report information right away or wait was quite discernible, offering no challenge. Although, I will say that there are a few nuggets of data I uploaded without believing they would have as large of a consequence as they did. 

[b]Short.[/b] There’s only a little over forty minutes of game play per episode, and with five episodes, this leads to roughly four hours of gameplay (assuming you don’t replay events). I follow a rule of thumb of at least $1 to 1 hour of gameplay, so in that regard, it’s a bit pricey. Just wait for a sale. 

[h1]Remark:[/h1] [b]Play in one sitting[/b] (or as close to that as possible, if you don't have a full 4-5 hours to dedicate to one game) The flow and length of the game lends itself to be optimally played in one sitting. game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
In the wake of a recent bombing, someone needs to be tasked to help investigate the suspected bombers. That someone is you. You are in charge of what goes in the system and what doesn't. But is there more to it? Is there a group planning it all together, or just one person? Do you paint them as terrorists or do you leave out enough information to show them as innocent?

[h1]Welcome to Orwell[/h1]
Orwell is one of those stories that is best to go blind in, since it is the most effective the first time. Hearing or seeing anything that is related to the main story, especially the end, ruins how you would play. But why? You are playing yourself, a new recruit of a programed named Orwell tasked to investigate suspicious people regarding the recent bombing. Through, which I wished happened more, a cutscene perfectly showing why and what this game is with only visuals. If you read 1984 Orwell is similar to how the government watches their people as it was influenced from George Orwell's books.

[h1]Datachunk Uploaded[/h1]
Down to it's core, you only read highlighted items, or datachunks, and dragging them to profiles for uploading. But there is much more if you are willing. Datachunks are meant to be evaluated, is this noteworthy to put on someone's profile? Do you purposefully make someone look worse or better? Should you upload every little thing? The game tried to put you in this mindset by your supervisor's comments and by conflicting datachunks (represented by a yellow highlight) to show you can't upload every little thing. Of course, there are datachunks needed to continue. Most of the time it is very apparent the datachunk is needed as it gives something new you can look through, solve a conflicting datachunk, or a sound cue picks up. This is all combined to represent how you view the situation. How you view the people you were tasked to investigate. How you have an influence on how their life will go after Orwell injected you into their lives. Sure, they do make their own decisions, but you have the power to have them forever be seen as a threat by the government.

Your first playthrough is key. It is how you would react in this situation, not how some character would. You do not know anything except what you gather. All other playthroughs after that is to see what could have happened if you did something differently. Anything you know about the main storyline ruins how you make decisions in the game. So I do recommend knowing as little as possible to get the most out of it.

I suppose Orwell is too easy. You have a supervisor meant to guide you, not only in Orwell but to guide your progress through the main storyline. It is very easy to just scroll down till you see phrases or words highlighted. Trying to find conflicting datachunks quickly to get past. While there is nothing stopping you, Orwell does try to encourage you to read. The many articles and websites you visit build the world as you continually gain access. In a way, the people you investigate brings you into the world as you unknowingly destroy theirs each datachunk at a time. There has been arguments about taking away the automatic highlighting, as why should you be hired if they have a system that does it, but there is too much that one can assume is needed. It could easily become entering random phrases or words till you get it right. So this way of highlighting does take away this confusion of what is and isn't noteworthy in a wall of text or conversations.

[h1]Sound[/h1]
There's limited sounds to Orwell, having background music and computer sounds. The background soundtrack never really changes until something notewrothy and important comes into view. While computer sounds symbolizes actions, such as a sound of a phone for a phone call and a click as datachunks are being entered.

[h1]Visuals[/h1]
While you do stare at a screen of your computer, Orwell has an interesting style when it comes to pictures. They build people with polygons. This gives an interesting visual that pops out when surrounded by text and brightening up the screen. The opening cutscene is one of the places that does not primarily showcase this style, going for more of an shaded outline. While the visuals are minimal, it does look appealing.

[h1]Performance[/h1]
Orwell easily runs well. Only having a few seconds of loading in the beginning of each chapter to load everything. There also seems to be a rare bug, not allowing the player to drag or view the preview of the datachunk. Thankfully, the datachunk is not needed to continue with the story, as it persists through the save, so it may only bother those who view it as an important datachunk to include in a profile.

[h1]Revisiting Orwell[/h1]
As said before, Orwell thrives on the first playthrough. After that, you know what's going to happen. You know what choices affects those you were assigned to. That first playthrough may be remembered as you replay, but so everthing major to the story. This is where you should look up guides as more playthroughs are solely for achievements that were off of the course you took. There are a total of three offical endings, all having subtle changed down the road. There's not much replayability but to see the difference the decisions have on the suspects.

[h1]Report[/h1]
+ Art style
+ Convincing characters; can easily be viewed as real people
+ Compelling story

+/- Your choice to see the world of Orwell
+/- Can be seen as constantly holding your hand

- The phone calls and texts are either too slow or too fast. You have to activate the certain call/text for it to start, breaking immersion since no one will wait till you come into the picture. If you are fast enough you can get two calls or texts (or a combination of the two) at the same time since you are likely to look at something else during other playthroughs. 

Orwell is one of those must play games. With the close hitting theme that may soon become reality. With all chapters released, you can easily have 2-3 hours of gamethrough per playthrough depending on how you choose to play. Orwell shows that you are being watched in some ways, even now, and that even you won't have the best interest for others if they have the possibility to be threats to society. Do not be afraid of going into Orwell this late, as I have and I was able to still get the most out of it.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
What to say about this game....

You play as a loyal outsourced investigator for "The Nation", and their new security program called Orwell.  The Orwell program is essentially surveillance designed to "keep the people of the Nation safe."  You investigate a group of individuals in an attempt to determine the culprit of a series of terrorist attacks.  Armed with the most invasive software at your disposal, you use every tool to spy on, and hopefully locate, all of the responsible parties.

Personally, it took me some time to get past the eerie feeling that what I was doing to spy on the lives of these virtual people wasn't too far off from what's probably been taking place in the world for a number of years.  This aspect of the game alone can make you feel almost uncomfortable with what you are doing.  However, your contact within Orwell does well, reminding you that what you are doing is for the safety of all.

The game itself, while it is a reading game at heart, does a really good job of pulling you in.  There are plot twists galore, and the game leaves you wanting to see the next piece of information you can dig up.

TL;DR - If you enjoy a dystopian setting, and enjoy reading-intensive games/mysteries, then I think you'll enjoy this game.  It is a short game; only a few hours, but it is definitely worth a few bucks.  I personally hope that they can use this to make a sequel of some kind.

If you are looking for a story in wich you just press highlighted pieces of text to progress this might be the game for you. If you where hoping for a game in wich you are asked to find out what happened using online surveilance you might want to look somewhere else.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
10/10 Drag and drop simulator.

The game sounded really interesting but after 2 hours of playtime I refunded it. The idea that you hunt for information and decide what to pass on and what to keep private is a nice way of turning a game into a subtle reference to personal bias. A clever idea that could have been great. The problem is that, certainly for the 2 hours I played, that simply wasn't the case. There is no hunting for information. It is handed to you on a plate. The basic routine is this:

A page of information is loaded and appears on the right of the screen. Important parts of the text are highlighted. Click the highlighted text and drag it to the Orwell upload facility on the left of the screen. Drag enough pieces of text and a new page of information is presented to you with highlighted parts. Drag and drop. New page. Drag and drop. New page.

You will discover social media handles. Great, now you can hunt the person down and..oh wait, no their feed just gets presented to you with highlighted text. Drag and drop.

You manage to get the telephone number of a suspect. Now you can tap their line and listen in on their conversations. Oh wait, it just gets presented to you, no action required. Never mind, look, there's the symbol to say they are about to have a conversation. QUICK, check in and listen to them before they...oh wait, no. You can simply ignore the symbol for half an hour and then check it, because the messages only start when you open up the screen. If these really are terrorists, they are the most considerate ones on the planet as they refuse to start their conversation until you are listening in. Try to keep up? No need, go make a drink, come back and find the page of text. Ignore the drivel, the important bits are highlighted.  Drag and drop.

Still, your decisions about what to upload is really what the game is about. Except that even in those first 2 hours there were a few occasions where I decided not to upload something because it appeared to be out of context. A message displaying agressiveness or hatred of the state, but in the context of the document it seemed to be just social media waffle and not really genuine terrorist. So I didn't upload it. Result? Nothing. The game simply wouldn't progress until I uploaded it. The choice was removed. So after a while of hunting and finding no new clues I reluctantly uploaded the info and lo and behold a new page of information was presented to me. Drag and drop. Rinse and repeat.

Clearly a lot of people have found something great in this game and I truly love the concept but I cannot recommend it for what it claims to be.  If you are looking for the perfect Drag and Drop Simulator to spend your evenings on though, you can't go wrong here.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
What a wasted opportunity.

I went into this game wanting to like it - I really did. To be clear - I played through the entire game, finishing each of the 5 chapters.

Orwell is ostensibly a game about a surveillance state gone terribly wrong - but almost at every opportunity, it fails to make any meaningful point and constantly gets in its own way.

It starts bad. Rather than giving you, as a player, the agency to incriminate and potentially ruin the lives of the people you are surveilling, the game immediately puts you at arms-length. You are nothing more than a data collector with the ability to find and store information, but not make any meaningful analysis or conclusions about this data. Worse, it pairs you with the clumsily-written and drearily heavy-handed Symes - the *actual* investigator, who acts on the information you upload and is a constant source of awkward, immersion-breaking, and stupid commentary. 

It's true that, in principle, the data you choose to upload can affect the lives and outcomes of the people whose privacy you're invading - the trouble is that there's no real incentive to do so. Oftentimes, you must upload certain pieces of data in order to move the story along - which makes sense, because you're nothing more than a glorified data monkey clicking blue text and throwing it into a database. If you choose to hide a piece of information, it's not clear whether or not you'll be able to progress through the story. If you get something wrong (in the extremely limited range of things you are even allowed to get wrong), there are few consequences - an issue exacerbated by how distanced you are from everything that goes down. You don't really get to make the call, figure out the deduction, or even choose whether or not you should be wielding the awesome power you do. You either progress the story, or you don't - Symes is the one who gets to actually decide.

What's worse is that each of the characters in the game are utterly unlikable - the crimes you investigate them for are legitimate crimes that hurt real innocents and pose genuine dangers to the society in which they inhabit - the moral quandary that this game should so naturally lend itself to (the invasion of privacy, the loss of intimacy, that everybody is a criminal under mass surveillance, etc.,) is utterly and absolutely wasted. Instead, you are railroaded through a specific set of documents, webpages, and chats (not giving you any opportunity to actually deduce anything) in which not one of the horribly written characters manages to endear themselves.

Ultimately, this game is trying to tell you two stories - a by the numbers B-grade mystery plot filled with unlikable and annoying characters, and a study of the evolution of mass surveillance in an increasingly tech-focussed society. In so doing, they tell neither one well. They did an incredible disservice to a barely-interesting character study of modern revolutionaries, and an even greater disservice to the core (and seemingly obvious!) issues with state-driven, indiscriminate surveillance.

Let's not even start with the UI. What begins as a somewhat interesting ability to listen in on conversations quickly becomes a tiresome and arduous chore - there are a couple of moments in which listening in on a conversation live makes sense, but these moments are few and far between. For the most part, you are treated to a disastrously slow chat message filled with stilted dialogue and unfortunate Fellow Kids idioms, or an equally slow voice transcription. I quickly began to dread these moments, rather than feel the rush of uncovering a potential clue.

At no point do you feel like a data wizard, an unscrupulous detective, or even a curious and detached researcher. You just feel bored. 

Orwell is, despite its polished presentation, a total and undeniable bust. 

Desperately trying to cram all of the social commentary it should have been exploring over the entire game into its final chapter, it fails to make a meaningful statement about mass surveillance and the police state. 

Having written shallow, stupid, stereotypical characters with zero likable traits or humanizing aspects (each of whom are also genuine suspects in an act of actual terrorism) it fails to present a compelling character study of the 21st-century revolutionary.

By railroading you during every part of the core gameplay loop and anchoring you at the waist with a bumbling, intrusive character (who gets to make *all* the calls and draw all the *actual* conclusions), they fail to provide a satisfying, thrilling, or even baseline interesting detective experience.

Finally, by forgetting the most fundamental principles in their clunky, limited, and careless design, they failed to provide an even halfway tolerable interface. 

I didn't even get to enjoy interacting with the game.

Orwell is a disaster. You will get nothing from it, no insight, no emotion, no deductions, and no surprises. It wastes every bit of the opportunity it had to say something meaningful.

This is my Two Minutes Hate - and Orwell deserves every second of it.

I expected to have to do more "detective work", but this is just a choices-don't-make-sense-but-they-matter experience.  Especially in the final chapter, I had little clue what I was supposed to accomplish, and then suddenly I accomplished something and the game was over.

If I could give this a Thumbs-Sideways, I would.  There are a few interesting "scenes" and moments that were surprising, but as it stands, I didn't feel like I was enjoying myself.  Just uploading "datachunks" and waiting for the game to find more datachunks to be uploaded.  Occasionally I had to decide between two conflicting pieces of data, but those choices were less-than-half of the game.  Maybe one-third of the game is "decisions" like that, and the rest is just dragging datachunks from one side of the screen to the other.  Or in some cases, deciding NOT to drag a datachunk from one side of the screen to the other, because it might be misunderstood by your superiors. For example, one comment on a website in-game says "oh no! the torture! ;)" in a playful manner about being bribed with muffins, but if you upload it your boss takes it to mean LITERAL TORTURE and freaks out about it.  So you're told to upload "all the relevant data" but then have no say in how it gets interpreted or used, which impacts upon the relevance of said data.

If you like games that try to make political-statements about things, this is probably up your alley.  I just wanted to solve puzzles, connect clues, etc.  The game highlights all the relevant information, and then connects it to things for you.  Not TERRIBLE, but not what I expected or hoped for. :(

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Creepy and well-written, Orwell tells the tale of what happens when the state gets unfettered access to your communication data, whether that be from the telephone or the internet. It's very topical, but it should be added that the scope of the access you have makes the recent "Snooper's Charter" in the UK look like lightweight. Nevertheless, your ability to screw with people's lives really hits home, especially when the twist at the end is revealed and all the consequences of your actions - and how misinterpreted data can be overblown - is laid bare.


That said, the game stays rather neutral in its moralising. It's clear the developers are anti-surveillance, as those *for* it would find the moral ambiguity of this game inconvenient, but they are not trying to whack you over the head with ideology. If you decide to come to the conclusion that, despite being messy at times, surveillance is a necessary evil then this game allows you to come to that conclusion. But it's going to push the extremes of what all-encompassing surveillance can do before it lets you come to that conclusion.

And while the politics of this game are clearly unavoidable, Orwell is also a pretty neat detective story, if not very typical. Instead of being in the front line looking for evidence, your sleuthing is invisible, but otherwise it has all the hallmarks of a good whodunnit, including red herrings, characters with strong motivations, and a twist at the end.

I'm not sure what else to say, really. It's pretty good and I happily recommend it.

[h1] DISCLAIMER: This is a full review, and NOT a first impressions review like all my other reviews, if you want a better full review, then please read better reviews then mine [/h1]

[quote] PLEASE NOTE: This review is being cast as a full review and not a first impressions review because the main bulk of the game is finished, although Orwell does have a story mode, it has different endings and choices, hence, this review is being cast as full because the main bulk of the game is complete, so please, think before you comment! Enjoy :) [/quote]

Orwell is a game developed by Osmotic Studios and published by Surpise Attack Games. Orwell is a compelling detective story that questions your morals, tugs your heart strings, and leaves you stunned. It has an intriguing plot that keeps you telling yourself "just one more episode..."

It does have some interesting characters who are easy to become attached to but not for long due to its short story and the game is intellectually satisfying. The game expects to absorb the world it has built and use deductive reasoning to back up your decisions and lines of investigation, basically meaning, it doesn't treat you like an idiot

However, Orwell is a fairly short game, finishing just one story with one ending in 2-3 hours is pretty damn short and currently there are no revising chapters and changing decisions. You have to create a new save from the beginning to pick different choices, however the developers have stated that they will change this in the near future with a patch

Orwell plays similar to a detective visual novel. If you are looking for flashy cutscenes and first/third person character control, then this is not the game for you. You are an intelligence agent working at your computer, and that is how you will experience this world. In my opinion, you do not need fancy graphics to appreciate the depth of this amazing story!

Orwell pays homage to one of the greatest writers of all time; George Orwell himself who has created some classic literary works such as Animal Farm and 1984 which this is inspired from!

[h1] RECOMMENDED :) [/h1]

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This is a difficult one to critique because whether or not you like it is mainly dependent on whether you like the narrative and how it is told. I’m not going to pretend that I know a huge amount about a good story well told, so when it comes to my thoughts on said story, take them with a grain of salt. Before I discuss that though, let’s talk about the game a bit.

[h1]“Interactive” Story[/h1]

In context, you are supposed to be a sort of investigator searching for clues about persons of interest via their emails, social media feeds, and phone conversations. I wouldn’t use the word “investigate” to describe the gameplay. Every import piece of information is already highlighted for you and you just need to drag-and-drop them to the appropriate location. When it comes selecting which documents you want to search through, there are indicators that tell which ones have important data-chunks. You don’t really have to read through the documents and phone texts unless you want story context.

This does streamline the gameplay experience, though. With a lot of story based adventure or point-and-click games, there is a risk of getting stuck at one part and losing all immersion in indirection proportion to mounting frustration. Orwell doesn’t have this problem as it is always very clear where you are supposed to look and this keeps a smooth pacing. As I mentioned earlier, this does contribute to the whole experience not feeling much like a traditional game as it feels much more like a guided tour of the characters and narrative progression. Perhaps a system where you have to highlight pieces of text you feel are important, and if you got the right piece then the story could progress? That may have been the original idea, but that could lead to many frustrations if you just barely missed the part of a quote you were supposed to get.

The only real gameplay in here is when there are two pieces of data that conflict with each other and you have to decide which one to submit to your superior. This could come in the form of two phone conversations by a character where one conversation makes him sound violent and the other makes him sound peaceful. Which one you submit will determine if that character gets arrested later in the story. This factors into a bit of a moral choice system regarding whether you try to paint the main characters and virtuous activists or terrorists. I feel an opportunity was missed to have more greatly divergent storylines to make the player feel like they have a real impact on the world. As it stands, your decisions only change minor events and what ending you get, with most of the heavy decision making existing in the last episode only.

[h1]Interactive “Story”[/h1]

With everything I’ve had to say about the gameplay thus far, you may be a bit perplexed as to why I recommend Orwell. Once again, this isn’t a typical [i]game[/i]. It’s a story with a bit more user control over the pace at which you progress through it. So how is the story?

Pretty good, actually.

The subject matter: government surveillance, is very topical and the game does a good job of showing the many different angles and opinions that people have about it. From those that try to peacefully discuss the issue, publicly criticize it, or are indifferent to it, every character seems believable and for the most part are consistent. The plot is revealed at a steady pace and is able to constantly engage. Appropriate music cues help to reinforce when something drastic has just taken place or when a particularly important piece of data is discovered and it does a good job of drawing you in. The last episode starts to deteriorate when the story starts to massively diverge and the amount of documents and computers to search through becomes overwhelming compared to the rest of the story.

While the data chunks are the most important piece of the story, there is a lot of text to sift through and it fleshes out the characters and game world quite well. A lot of it is unnecessary and for a while I thought that a small sub-plot about terrorism in another country was going to turn out to be a major plot device because the game kept bringing it up, but that ended up being nothing important. Also, documents and conversations are never deleted, so you are free to browse through them at your leisure and one small link could lead you down a rabbit’s hole worth of information. Having assessed these can be handy if the story calls for you to investigate those links and you’re already familiar with them, which does occasionally make you feel like a real investigator.

There are a few off moments when the characters don’t feel believable because we only see them communicate via text. Towards the end, [spoiler]everyone is panicking because they have discovered the Orwell system and can’t figure out how to deal with it,[/spoiler] and sometimes text just isn’t the best way to convey those sorts of emotions. These are hardly deal breakers though because what it boils down to is that whenever I would start the game up, it wasn’t because I felt some obligation to finish it. It was because I wanted to know what happens next. And no matter how many trivial nit-picks I have with the story, that single fact means I have to acknowledge that the story is engaging.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]

Orwell is a story, and not much of a game. Whatever gameplay is present serves entirely to incrementally progress you through the story and not present any kind of and challenge by itself. An experience like this lives and dies on whether or not its story is engaging which, to me at least, it certainly was.

review_text_raw:
[b]My playtime:[/b] 10h (based on steam, 100% achievement; 2.5x playthrough)
[b]Grindy Achievement(s):[/b] No.
[b]Optional Achievement(s):[/b] Yes (17 achievements).
[b]Difficult Achievement(s):[/b] No.

[h1]Intro[/h1]
[i]Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You[/i] is a massive information gathering system where you, an investigator, is taking a role in sorting the relevant data and fix conflicting data that the system gathered to assist a crime. The game has story branching that persists over 5 chapters.

[b]Pros:[/b]
- 5 chapters
- Multiple endings and story branching that persists over the chapters
- Clean and fresh-looking interface
- You can restart a chapter after you finished the game

[b]Cons:[/b]
- Phone calls and chat animations take a very long time to finish
- Some clues are too hard to deduce unless if you know the full story
- You can't press the button to show conflicting data sometimes

[h1]Should you buy this game?[/h1]
[b]Yes.[/b]
[i]If you like to read or stalk people, you should buy this game. You also can buy it at a discount if you think that the playtime isn't worth the full price.[/i]

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[h1]In-Depth Review[/h1]

[h1]Graphics[/h1]
The interface is clean and fresh-looking. I like how the summary that is shown at the end of the chapter is introduced; it looks like the workboard in my office except that it's way cleaner.

As someone who likes to try something by doing it firsthand, I don't find the design to be confusing. The portal section looks like your regular website, the message section looks like your regular chat app, and the device section looks like the simpler version of your device.

I'm also impressed by how the dev showed the photos; it looks like a fragmented version of our faces and it looks so detailed even though it's not. The important facial like eyes and hair is shown although most details are blurred and fragmented.

The cutscene at the prologue skipped a few frames to me though, although I don't have any trouble in understanding the story because of that.

[h1]Story[/h1]
The story is being told by several conversations of your "adviser", someone who deduce things based on your findings, and whatever you read when you try to find clues, which are mostly from chat and phone calls.

Even though most conversations are held this way, I didn't find the main story to be confusing. Even if you couldn't understand the story, the "adviser" will give you some sort of info as to what is happening so you should be fine as long as you don't skip it. There's also a summary at the end of the chapter if you want to keep track of things.

There are several branchings in the game, either minor or major. I find the conversation between the branches to be smooth although some parts confused me since I didn't know the whole story at that moment. You need to play several playthroughs throughout the game to get all the major story branches and understand the whole story.

The thing is, there is no good or bad ending in this game; it's all about your opinion. You think what you think is good and bad. You also can deduce the whole story if you want or you can just understand the main story and be done with it.

[h1]The game[/h1]
[b]Features[/b]
There are 3 sections where you do most of your work: portal, message, and device. The in-game name is different, but I can't seem to recall the actual name since you don't need to know about the name to use it.

The portal consists of several web pages that you can access. The pages that you can access are limited to the system and more will show up as you unlock more clues.

The message, on the other hand, is a bit different. A message, either chat, email, or phone, will show up at certain times and you're allowed to wire-tap their chat and calls in real-time. The thing is, the chat speed is very slow. You can speed up the phone chat speed a bit although I still want it to be faster. It's taking too much time to listen to it especially when you're replaying your playthrough.

The device can be activated after you obtain a serial number of the target's device. You can access all files in the device, whether it's from a desktop or phone.

[b]Investigation[/b]
The suspect will have a profile page that you can fill with data. These data can be obtained by browsing through the 3 sections I mentioned. The data that you can take will be highlighted, either in blue or yellow.

Blue-colored means that there is no conflict with the data and yellow means that the data contradicts with other data. The game also has an option to show the conflicting data although I find that it's not working sometimes.

The thing is, you have freedom in choosing whatever you submit. I thought that I should fill all of the highlighted data in blue for complete profiling, but it's actually the opposite. All the data that you fill will be useful for the advisor's judgment and other people's fate, so you should decide carefully on what you submit.

Some data that you submit will change the story greatly, some are not. Although probably considered a "short" game by most (I played through the entire thing in one sitting in about 4-5 hours), I thrououghly enjoyed this game! I was surprised with how well written it was, each character had a distinct personality that I felt I could connect with, making the subject matter all the more real.

It is not without its problems though. The biggest issue I noticed was in determining what pieces of data needed to be uploaded to advance the story. In the beginning they flat out tell you that you don't have to upload everything, however I often found myself encountering pieces of information I felt not pertinent to the subject matter or specifics of the investigation at the time, but without uploading theses, the story would not progress. I am not sure if this is me misunderstanding the mechanics, a flaw in the story scripting, or a comment on how invasive survailance really can be.

Although most characters were well written, I felt like a few too many were "bi-polar", totally changing personality and actions out of nowhere. Again, I'm not sure if this was how it was written from the start, or if I uploaded enough of the "right" snippets to trigger these outcomes.

Overall, very well written, although I'm not sure how much replay value it has. I'd give it a solid 8/10

review_text_raw:
I really enjoyed Papers, Please.  I really enjoyed Beholder.  The "authoritarian minion simulator" is a really interesting game concept, and I wanted to like it, but Orwell just bored me.

It should be picking up clues to things that should go together, but gameplay is all highlighted drag & drop.  And thus I found myself not really caring.

It doesn't help that the drag & drop simulated internet is just enough of a facsimile to remind me I could be doing this on the real internet and it would be easier (albeit dead internet making it slightly harder in 2026).

You could quite literally start an X account and start reading posts by (let's see if my review makes it to being posted now!) Nick Shirley about mass fraud in the US or Rupert Lowe about mass... problems... in the UK and look for crimes actually being committed or covered up, then go and look at the names/places/groups in the reports they put out and start doing your own investigative work and start posting publicly available but little-known connections as you find them... and it would be both meaningful and less boring.  You wouldn't be an authoritarian minion, you'd just be someone doing basic investigative citizen journalism (or wonky tisming), but it's just finding connections.  Every "this you?" tweet where someone researches a political/celebrity timeline to find contradictory positions is more interesting that Orwell.

And that's why Orwell is weak.  Rather than go "huh, what's out there", it prompts the next link on a fake web, with things to drag and drop, over and over.

I wanted to like it, but found the story not hooking me in, the gameplay a tedious, railroading copy of the real internet, and overall just bleh.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I've only played one case. Maybe it gets better but I already hate it. This is a game that saw [i]Papers Please[/i] and a Telltale game and thought: these should be one thing. They shouldn't. It wants to have the humanism of a game that is mostly just a postmodern exploration of character ([i]Her Story, Analogue: A Hate Story[/i]), but it also wants you to make binary data choices on which set of data to pass on to your superior without being given enough information to know how it will be interpreted.

[i]Papers Please[/i] presents very clear outcomes for the majority of your choices and the moral weight they have and gives a context for why a choice must be made anyway.  By presenting the status quo of a job which you must do for a family who could starve, the game allows for depth of story, a context for why things must be as they are and real stakes for the choices that are made.

Telltale games often don't pre-empt the outcomes of your choices, but often these choices are superfluous because what matters is the character drama. But the thing is that the games sensationalize these choices and make them feel like they could matter, even when they don't. This character could die instead of this one, you might find out a different set of information, but the structure of the story and the characters' movement through it remains intact. 

When you mash them up what you get is a completely unnuanced yes-no/good-bad moral choice system ala Fable in a world that resembles the real one too closely for that to not be cringe-worthy. Only the binary isn't good/bad because as someone who is already spying on someone and potentially ruining their life just to test if you can get access to the next document by adding chunks that seem only tangentially related but will be interpreted as reason to call the police, you're always bad. And if that's what the game's political critique boils down to, then I got it. Thumbs up.

"Are they really terrorists?" the game's description asks. And the answer is no. I could have guessed that from the bugged out clip following her getting on a bus that only played the second time I started a new game because the first one I hit a dead end and had no choice but to just start adding data at random hoping something would trigger only to have to google and find out it was a known bug and I just had to restart from the start. So thanks, I hate it.
